title: Bracts and beyond – spikelet diversity in the wider Poales: a commentary on ‘Hygroscopic awns and inflorescence architecture in a wind-pollinated Australian monocot: functional convergence with grasses’
content: The Poales, one of the largest angiosperm orders and which contains grasses, bromeliads, rushes and sedges, show great evolutionary success in dry and open environments, attributed largely to the pollination and seed dispersal strategies facilitated by the architecture of the spikelet (Linder et al., 2018). The spikelet is the fundamental unit of grass inflorescences, comprising flowers surrounded by bracts (Clayton, 1990). In many grasses, spikelets also bear an awn, a bristle-like extension of the lemma that has evolved multiple times across the grasses and exhibits striking diversity in both form and function (Patterson et al., 2025). While mostly considered a grass innovation, spikelets have evolved more than once in the Poales including in the Restionaceae and Cyperaceae (Linder and Rudall, 2005).
